<Rep. Jared Huffman>: H.R. 7487, the Rural Jobs and Hydropower Expansion Act, would amend the Reclamation Project Act of 1939, authorizing all non-federal hydropower development projects associated with Bureau of Reclamation (Reclamation) facilities to utilize the Department of the Interior's Lease of Power Privilege (LOPP) permitting process in lieu of the permitting and licensing process used by the Federal Energy Regulatory Commission (FERC).
Congress tasked FERC with overseeing most non-federal hydropower development in the United States and designed the Federal Power Act (FPA) licensing process to balance energy production with other important public interests, including the protection of Tribal reservations, federal public lands, and fish and wildlife resources. The Interior Department's hydropower permitting process does not provide clear equivalents to the FPA in statute. Under current law, the development of hydropower by non-federal entities on Reclamation projects is permitted by both Reclamation and FERC. Jurisdiction is defined under Memorandums of Understanding, with Reclamation maintaining exclusive jurisdiction over Reclamation facilities authorized by Congress for federal hydropower purposes, while FERC is responsible for permitting at Reclamation facilities not originally authorized for federal hydropower development.
H.R. 7487 would significantly expand the use of the Interior Department's statutorily less protective permitting process for non-federal hydropower development at Reclamation water facilities, including many projects that would otherwise be licensed by FERC under the FPA. Specifically, FPA section 4(e) requires FERC, before licensing or relicensing a hydropower project affecting a federal reservation--including Tribal trust lands and many federal public lands--to determine that a project will not interfere or be inconsistent with the purposes for which a federal reservation was created. FERC is also required to include hydropower license conditions prescribed by the federal agency with jurisdiction over that reservation to ensure its adequate protection and use. FPA section 18 also gives the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service and the National Marine Fisheries Service authority to prescribe mandatory fishway conditions for projects that would affect fish passage. FPA section 10(j) also requires FERC to include license conditions to protect, mitigate damage to, and enhance fish and wildlife affected by a licensed hydropower project, based on recommendations from federal and state fish and wildlife agencies, unless FERC determines those recommendations are inconsistent with the FPA or other law. Together, these provisions give Tribes, federal land managers, and resource agencies enforceable tools to protect Tribal rights and resources, federal reservations, fish passage, recreation and other environmental resources during the hydropower licensing process.
While Reclamation regulations may incorporate similar protections into the permitting process, the Reclamation Project Act of 1939 does not provide the same protection as the FPA. H.R. 7487 would remove many non-federal hydropower projects from the enforceable statutory protections of the FPA and place them under the Interior Department's less protective permitting process without requiring similar safeguards.
Congress can support hydropower development and improve the licensing process without weakening major existing safeguards for Tribes, public lands, and our native fish and wildlife. In an effort to work with the Majority, the Minority offered an amendment that would preserve existing FPA safeguards for non-federal hydropower development projects affecting Tribes, treaty rights, fish and wildlife and other public resources, while still allowing the bill to consolidate licensing at the Interior Department. Unfortunately, our amendment was not adopted. For these reasons, I oppose this legislation.
Jared Huffman,
Ranking Member.
